title: Four eras of San Francisco tech culture
gist: Noah Smith sketches four eras of San Francisco tech culture (Rebel, Corporate, Interregnum, AI) and notes that Trump allies are now targeting Dario Amodei and effective altruism, wrongly in his view, since Rationalists drive AI safety. The text is a paywalled excerpt that stops at the start of the Corporate Era, so only the prehistory and the Rebel Era are covered.

insights.claim: Trump allies are targeting Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as the face of AI doomerism, and a White House memo by a Trump political adviser frames effective altruism as a fringe, cultish movement that 'built the AI-doom pipeline'.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Political targeting of a frontier lab's CEO raises regulatory and reputational risk for Anthropic specifically.
insights.quote: Effective altruism “built the AI-doom pipeline,” states the memo, which was penned by a Trump political adviser

insights.claim: The White House and press are misidentifying the AI-safety group: the real AI safety obsessives are the Rationalists, descended from the 1990s Extropians, while EA is a largely separate movement that joined AI safety later.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Political attacks aimed at EA may misfire, so the policy effect on AI safety discourse may be smaller than headlines imply.
insights.quote: the AI safety obsessives that the White House is taking aim at are the Rationalists, who are descended from a group of 1990s futurists called the Extropians
insights.locator: I’ve never been an Effective Altruist

insights.claim: EA's influence on the AI safety discussion is probably much smaller than people think.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests overweighting EA in policy analysis of AI safety is a mistake.
insights.quote: its influence on the AI safety discussion is probably a lot less than people think
insights.locator: I’ve never been an Effective Altruist

insights.claim: San Francisco tech culture since 2001 falls into four eras: the Rebel Era (2001-2012), the Corporate Era (2012-2019), the Interregnum (2020-2022), and the AI Era (2022-present).
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Gives a lens for how cultural and political center of gravity in tech shifts with capital flows.
insights.locator: Today what I wanted to do

insights.claim: The tech industry began on the Peninsula around Stanford (Shockley in Mountain View in 1955, then Fairchild and Intel), and San Francisco was originally a marginal player that rose via media startups and Wired, founded there in 1993.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Historical context for the shift of tech's center from Sand Hill Road suburbs to the city.

insights.claim: In the 2000s, starting a company in SF instead of the Peninsula marked you as a rebel; the city's alternative tech culture was laid-back, liberal and product-focused, with Twitter as its most famous product.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Shows how location choice signals culture and founder type.
insights.locator: If you went up to SF

insights.claim: The Rebel Era's core ideology held that social hierarchies rest on information control and the internet would liberate humanity, with the Electronic Frontier Foundation, not Rationalism or LessWrong, as its key touchstone.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Tracks the evolution of tech's political ideology, relevant to how tech engages policy today.
insights.quote: The tech rebels of the 2000s believed that social hierarchies were based on information control, and that if they simply broke that control, the hierarchies would be overturned.

insights.claim: The Rebel Era pushed tech leftward as Marc Benioff and others entered politics on the liberal side, reinforced by education polarization that made most engineers liberal.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Explains tech's historical political alignment, a baseline for measuring current realignment.

insights.claim: The Rebel Era could not last because its bohemian, flat culture depended on a lack of money; when money arrived, SF tech was transformed into the Corporate Era.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Capital inflows reshape tech culture, a pattern likely repeating in the AI Era.
insights.quote: Its bohemian, socially flattened culture was always predicated on a lack of money, and when money came in, SF tech was transformed.
